title: Brightline Robotics: corporate income tax
participant_role: Tax associate at a CPA firm
judge_role: Chief financial officer of BRIGHTLINE ROBOTICS, INC., a calendar-year C corporation

difficulty.rationale: Book to taxable income, 21% tax and the tax entry.

scenario:
You are to assume the role of a tax associate at a CPA firm. The chief financial officer (judge) of BRIGHTLINE ROBOTICS, INC., a client, has asked you to help finish the company's federal income tax work for the year.

BRIGHTLINE ROBOTICS, INC. designs and sells warehouse robots. The company is a C corporation with a calendar tax year. Its accounting staff has closed the books and reported pre-tax income for the year. During the year the company made quarterly estimated federal tax payments, which the staff recorded as Prepaid Income Taxes.

The chief financial officer (judge) assumed the company's federal tax would simply be 21% of the income shown on its income statement. After reviewing the year's records, you noticed that several items included in book income are treated differently for tax purposes. The chief financial officer (judge) is surprised that the tax return and the income statement will not show the same income and wants to understand why.

The chief financial officer (judge) also needs the year-end income tax entry for the financial statements, wants to know what must be filed and when, and has asked how the company can avoid legal trouble and penalties related to taxes.

[Brightline Robotics tax information: see exhibits]

You must:
- Explain why taxable income differs from book income
- Calculate taxable income and federal income tax
- Record the year-end income tax entry
- Identify the tax return, its due date and the balance due
- Explain legal considerations and risk management for taxes

You will present your information to the chief financial officer (judge) in a role-play to take place in the chief financial officer's office. The chief financial officer (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented your information and have answered the chief financial officer's (judge's) questions, the chief financial officer (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

judge_questions: Can we just leave the fine off our books so we don't have to explain it?
If we file an extension, do we still have to pay by April 15?

solution.overview: A strong answer explains why book and taxable income differ, adjusts $500,000 of book income for the nondeductible half of meals, the fine and tax-exempt municipal interest to reach taxable income of $495,000 and federal tax of $103,950, and records the tax entry that clears $90,000 of prepaid taxes and sets up $13,950 payable. The presenter then identifies Form 1120, its April 15 due date and the extension rule, and explains legal considerations and tax risk management.

answer: Book income follows accounting rules (GAAP); taxable income follows the tax law
Some expenses are not fully deductible: only 50% of business meals, and fines are never deductible
Some income is not taxable, such as interest on municipal bonds
These permanent differences are adjusted to move from book income to taxable income
Start with book income $500,000
Add back the nondeductible half of meals $10,000 and the fine $5,000
Subtract tax-exempt municipal interest $20,000
Effective rate on book income = 103,950 / 500,000 = about 20.8%
Record the full year's tax as Income Tax Expense of $103,950
Clear the $90,000 of estimated payments out of Prepaid Income Taxes
Record the remaining $13,950 as Income Taxes Payable
The entry balances: debits $103,950 = credits $103,950

by_task.task: Return, due date and balance due
answer: A C corporation files Form 1120
Due April 15 for a calendar-year company (15th day of the 4th month)
An extension (Form 7004) gives 6 more months to file, but not to pay
Balance due = 103,950 minus 90,000 = $13,950, payable by April 15
Tax avoidance (legal planning within the law) is allowed; tax evasion (hiding income or false deductions) is a crime
Late filing or late payment brings penalties and interest
Keep records while the IRS can audit, generally 3 years after filing
Reduce risk: second-preparer review, documented positions, a deadline calendar and on-time estimated payments

judge_question_answers.question: Can we just leave the fine off our books so we don't have to explain it?
answer: No: the fine is a real expense and must be recorded, or the financial statements are misstated
Hiding it would mislead lenders, investors and auditors and could be treated as fraud
The tax return reconciles book income to taxable income, so the fine appears there as an add-back anyway
Recording it honestly and fixing the cause of the fine is the better risk management

judge_question_answers.question: If we file an extension, do we still have to pay by April 15?
answer: Yes: an extension gives more time to file the return, not more time to pay
Pay the estimated $13,950 balance by April 15 when filing the extension
Unpaid tax after April 15 is charged interest and a late payment penalty
The completed Form 1120 is then due by the extended date

key_concepts.definition: Income before taxes as reported on the financial statements under accounting rules (GAAP).
Income calculated under the tax law, on which income tax is charged. It often differs from book income.
An item counted for book purposes but never for tax (or the reverse), such as fines, the nondeductible half of meals and municipal bond interest.
A flat 21% of a C corporation's taxable income.
Income tax expense divided by pre-tax book income; it shows the company's actual tax burden.
Tax paid during the year, usually quarterly, before the return is filed. They are recorded as Prepaid Income Taxes until the year's tax is known.
A liability for income tax owed but not yet paid at year end.
The federal income tax return for C corporations, due the 15th day of the 4th month after year end (April 15 for calendar-year companies).
Form 7004 gives a corporation 6 more months to file its return, but tax is still due by the original due date.
Avoidance is legally reducing tax through planning; evasion is illegally hiding income or claiming false deductions.
The period during which the IRS can audit a return, generally 3 years after filing, which guides how long to keep records.

notes: State level because students must adjust book income for three permanent differences, record a three-line tax entry and explain filing and legal rules. Common mistakes: applying 21% to book income, adding back the full $20,000 of meals instead of half, and believing an extension also delays payment.

criteria.exceeds: Records the year-end entry (debit Income Tax Expense $103,950, credit Prepaid Income Taxes $90,000, credit Income Taxes Payable $13,950), explains that it clears the estimated payments and sets up the balance still owed, and confirms debits equal credits.
criteria.meets: Records debit Income Tax Expense $103,950, credit Prepaid Income Taxes $90,000 and credit Income Taxes Payable $13,950.
criteria.below: Uses the right accounts with a wrong amount, such as $105,000 of expense from taxing book income, or leaves out the Prepaid Income Taxes credit.
criteria.little: Gives no tax entry, or an entry with unrelated accounts.

criteria.exceeds: Calculates taxable income of $495,000 (500,000 + 10,000 half of meals + 5,000 fine minus 20,000 municipal interest) and tax of $103,950, identifies Form 1120 due April 15 with a Form 7004 extension of 6 months to file but not to pay, and states the $13,950 balance due by April 15.
criteria.meets: Calculates taxable income of $495,000 and tax of $103,950, and identifies Form 1120, the April 15 due date and the $13,950 balance due.
criteria.below: Makes a key error such as adding back the full $20,000 of meals (taxable income $505,000) or taxing book income, or cannot name the form or due date.
criteria.little: Does not calculate taxable income or tax, or cannot identify the return.

items.label: Discuss legal considerations in the finance industry

criteria.exceeds: Distinguishes legal tax avoidance from tax evasion (hiding income or false deductions, a crime), explains penalties and interest for late filing or payment, and notes records must be kept while the IRS can audit, generally 3 years after filing.
criteria.meets: Explains the difference between tax avoidance and tax evasion and that late filing or payment brings penalties and interest.
criteria.below: Mentions following the law in general terms without explaining avoidance, evasion or penalties.
criteria.little: Does not address legal considerations, or suggests hiding items from the IRS is acceptable.

items.label: Discuss legal considerations affecting risk management

criteria.exceeds: Recommends specific controls: a second-preparer review, documented tax positions, a deadline calendar, on-time estimated payments and records kept at least 3 years, and connects each to avoiding penalties, interest and legal exposure.
criteria.meets: Recommends at least two practical ways to reduce tax risk, such as review, a deadline calendar or on-time estimated payments.
criteria.below: Gives general advice to be careful without specific risk management steps.

items.label: Explain the nature of tax liabilities

criteria.exceeds: Explains that book income follows GAAP and taxable income follows tax law, names the three permanent differences (only 50% of meals deductible, fines never deductible, municipal bond interest not taxable), and shows the effective rate on book income is about 20.8%, not 21%.
criteria.meets: Explains why taxable income differs from book income and identifies the meals, fine and municipal interest adjustments.
criteria.below: Says book and tax income differ but cannot explain why, or treats the adjustments in the wrong direction.
criteria.little: Agrees with the CFO that tax is simply 21% of book income.

items.label: Critical Thinking: Reason effectively and use systems thinking

criteria.exceeds: Connects each permanent difference to taxable income, the $103,950 tax, the journal entry and the $13,950 balance due, showing how one step flows into the next.
criteria.meets: Reasons correctly from the exhibit to taxable income and the tax owed.
criteria.below: Reaches a conclusion without showing the reasoning, or misses how one step affects the next.

items.label: Problem Solving: Make judgments and decisions and solve problems

criteria.exceeds: Gives the CFO a clear action plan: book the tax entry, pay $13,950 by April 15, file Form 1120 or an extension, and put review and deadline controls in place.
criteria.meets: Gives clear next steps for recording, filing and paying the tax.
criteria.below: Gives advice that is partly correct or not clearly stated.

criteria.exceeds: Explains book versus taxable income and the tax entry in plain language the CFO can follow, in a logical order, with confident and professional delivery.
criteria.meets: Presents the differences, calculation, entry, filing rules and legal points clearly and in an organized way.
criteria.below: Presentation is hard to follow, relies on jargon, or skips steps.

items.label: Creativity and Innovation: Show evidence of creativity

criteria.exceeds: Uses a simple reconciliation from $500,000 book income to $495,000 taxable income, or a tax deadline calendar, and adds a useful idea such as reviewing estimated payments so the balance due is smaller next year.
criteria.meets: Organizes the information in a way that makes the tax picture easy to understand.
criteria.below: Presents the facts with little effort to make them engaging or easy to follow.
criteria.little: Shows no evidence of creativity or original thought.

items.label: Overall impression and responses to the judge's questions

criteria.exceeds: Answers both questions correctly and confidently: the fine is a real expense that must be recorded, hiding it would misstate the statements and could be treated as fraud, and it appears on the return as an add-back anyway; and an extension gives more time to file, not to pay, so the $13,950 must be paid by April 15 to avoid interest and a late payment penalty.
criteria.meets: Answers both questions mostly correctly, including that the fine must stay on the books and that payment is still due April 15.
criteria.below: Answers only one question correctly, or gives vague answers without the April 15 date or the $13,950 balance.
criteria.little: Cannot answer the judge's questions, or agrees to leave the fine off the books or says an extension delays payment.

key_points: Book income follows GAAP and taxable income follows tax law; permanent differences cause the gap
Taxable income = 500,000 + 10,000 (half of meals) + 5,000 (fine) minus 20,000 (municipal interest) = $495,000
Federal tax = 495,000 x 21% = $103,950 (effective rate on book income about 20.8%)
Entry: debit Income Tax Expense $103,950, credit Prepaid Income Taxes $90,000, credit Income Taxes Payable $13,950
A C corporation files Form 1120, due April 15; balance due 103,950 minus 90,000 = $13,950
An extension (Form 7004) gives 6 more months to file but not to pay
Tax avoidance is legal planning; tax evasion is a crime; reduce risk with review, a deadline calendar, on-time estimated payments and records kept at least 3 years
